title: Probability Density Function (PDF)
subtitle: Topic: Probability Density Function · Subject: Probability and Statistics · Seven illustrated questions on density versus point probability, normalization, integrating intervals, CDFs, Python midpoint integration, transformed PDFs and joint/conditional densities.
hero:
PROBABILITY DENSITY FUNCTION · PROBABILITY AND STATISTICS

Probability is the area under a density curve

Explore what a continuous density means, why its total area is one, how intervals become probabilities, and how CDFs, transformations and joint densities extend the same idea.

PDF curveProbability area

The height of a probability density is not itself a point probability. An interval’s probability is the area beneath the curve over that interval.

questions.stem: What does a probability density function (PDF) represent for a continuous random variable, and why does a positive density at an exact point not mean that point has positive probability?
options: A PDF assigns a direct probability to each measured value, and those individual probabilities add to one over all possible outcomes. A point with density 0.399 therefore has probability 39.9%, independent of the measurement's units.

A PDF expresses probability per unit of the variable, and probabilities come from areas across intervals. For an absolutely continuous distribution, an exact point has zero probability even when the density there is positive.

A PDF gives the cumulative chance of observing a value or anything smaller, so its value at one point already counts the full probability to that point. Integrating that curve would count the same outcomes twice.

A PDF measures how often a rounded instrument displays a particular recorded value, making its height equal to the probability of an exact real-valued outcome. Interval probabilities are computed by adding those point heights.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A probability density function describes how probability is spread over a continuous variable. The chance of an interval is the area under the density there; a single exact point has zero area and therefore zero probability for an absolutely continuous distribution. Density has inverse units and may be positive at that point. For example, a subway arrival-time error modeled as standard normal has f(0)≈0.399 per minute, but an error of exactly zero minutes has probability zero. An error within ±0.5 minute has about 38.3% probability.

A nonzero curve height does not make a single continuous value probable

Point heightFor the standard normal arrival error, f(0)≈0.399 per minute, but P(X=0)=0.
Interval areaThe chance of an error within half a minute of zero is about 38.3%.

A probability density function (PDF) gives density per unit of the measured variable, not the chance of one exact value. For an absolutely continuous distribution, every single point has probability zero, even if its density is positive. Probabilities require integration across intervals.

questions.stem: What conditions make a function a valid continuous probability density function, and how can a density larger than one still represent a valid distribution?
options: A valid PDF integrates to one across its support, but may take negative values provided positive and negative sections cancel. A height above one is acceptable because only the signed total area matters for probabilities.

A valid PDF stays between zero and one at every input and sums its heights to one over the support. Any density taller than one would assign more than 100% probability to a possible single observation.

A valid PDF has nonnegative values and a total area that equals the width of the support. A narrow interval may therefore use large density values because the final probability is obtained by normalizing that width.
A valid PDF is nonnegative and integrates to one across all possible values. Its height can exceed one on narrow support: uniform density five over [0,0.2] still has area 0.2×5=1.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A continuous PDF must be nonnegative almost everywhere and have total integral one. Its height is a density, not a probability, so there is no upper bound of one on individual density values. A narrow support can require a tall PDF. For example, a timer with a uniformly distributed rounding error between zero and 0.2 seconds has density five per second throughout that interval; its area is 0.2×5=1. A uniform error over two seconds has density 0.5 per second and also integrates to one.
questions.figure:
02 · VISUAL LESSON

Both wide and narrow PDFs have area one—even if one density exceeds one

Nonnegative densityTotal area equals 1Height may be greater than 1Axes have different scales

A valid continuous PDF must be nonnegative (except possibly at isolated irrelevant points) and integrate to one over its full support. Density height is measured per unit; there is no requirement that f(x) be at most one. A narrow uniform interval can therefore have a tall density.

questions.stem: How do you calculate the probability that a continuous variable lies between two boundaries using its PDF, and what is P(1<X<2) when f(x)=x/2 on [0,2]?
options: Integrate the density from one to two and divide the result by the two-unit support length. Since the rising triangular density reaches height one at the endpoint, this adjustment gives a probability of 0.375.
Subtract the values of the density at the interval endpoints, then multiply by the interval width. For f(x)=x/2, the resulting probability is (1−0.5)×1=0.50 because only endpoint heights contribute.
Integrate f(x)=x/2 from one to two to obtain the area under the curve. The integral [x²/4]₁² equals 1−0.25=0.75, representing three quarters of the total probability.
Average the density over its entire support and multiply by the chosen interval's width. Because the full triangle has average height 0.5, every interval of width one has probability 0.50.
questions.explanation: Explanation: For a continuous variable, the probability between boundaries a and b is the integral of its PDF over that interval. This counts the area under the graph. For f(x)=x/2 on [0,2], the full triangular area is one. Integrating from one to two gives [x²/4] from 1 to 2, or 1−0.25=0.75. For example, if a valve's calibrated rotation is more likely near two units than zero, the chance of a reading between one and two is 75%, not the average density height.
questions.figure:
03 · VISUAL LESSON

Integrating a sloping density gives an interval probability of 0.75

Integral method∫₁²(x/2)dx = [x²/4]₁² = 1−0.25 = 0.75.
Complement methodP(1<X<2) = 1−P(0<X<1) = 1−0.25.

For a continuous variable with density f(x), the chance of falling between a and b is the integral of f over that interval. Under f(x)=x/2 on [0,2], the full triangular area is one. The interval from one to two captures three quarters of that area.

questions.tag: Medium · Relationship between PDF and CDF
questions.stem: How is a continuous cumulative distribution function (CDF) related to its PDF, and how do you use the CDF to find P(0.2<X<0.8) when f(x)=2x on [0,1]?
options: The CDF accumulates PDF area up to x, and its derivative equals the density where differentiable. Here F(x)=x², so the interval probability is F(0.8)−F(0.2)=0.64−0.04=0.60.
The CDF records the density value at x and grows by adding the density only at observed sample points. Here F(x)=2x, so subtracting F(0.8)−F(0.2)=1.20 would need a probability cap.
The CDF accumulates probability to the right of x, so it decreases as x increases. Here F(x)=1−x², and the desired interval probability is F(0.8)−F(0.2)=−0.60.
The CDF is found by differentiating the PDF, and the PDF is recovered by integrating the CDF. Here F(x)=2 for all positive x, giving a zero difference between 0.2 and 0.8.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The CDF F(x)=P(X≤x) accumulates area beneath the PDF up to x. Where it is differentiable, F'(x)=f(x). Probabilities between two boundaries equal the difference of their cumulative probabilities. For f(x)=2x on [0,1], integration gives F(x)=x², so P(0.2
questions.figure:
04 · VISUAL LESSON

The CDF accumulates area; its derivative recovers the PDF

PDF: f(x)=2xCDF: F(x)=x²P(0.2<X<0.8)=0.60

The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is F(x)=P(X≤x), the area under the PDF up to x. Where differentiable, its derivative is the density. Either integrate the PDF between boundaries or subtract CDF values. For f(x)=2x on [0,1], F(x)=x².

questions.stem: How can Python numerically approximate probability under a normal PDF, and why must it integrate over an interval rather than use the density height at one point?
options: Python can calculate the normal density at each end of an interval and average those two heights, treating the result as the interval's probability. The midpoint rule is unnecessary because normal curves are symmetric.

Python can sum normal density values across thousands of inputs without multiplying by each subinterval width. The resulting sum is already a probability because a normalized density integrates to one across its support.

Python can use the midpoint rule to approximate the normal density but should divide by the interval length after summing the areas. This makes the answer a probability at the center, rather than an interval probability.
Python can partition an interval into pieces, evaluate the PDF at each midpoint, and sum height times width. For standard normal Z, integration from −1 to 1 yields about 0.682689 while P(Z=0)=0.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Numerical integration estimates probability by dividing an interval into many small pieces and summing each piece's width times the PDF at its midpoint. For a smooth normal density, this approximates area accurately with enough slices. The density height at one point is not the probability of that exact value. For example, a lab may model standardized instrument error by Z∼N(0,1). The Python demonstration gives P(−1
questions.figure:
05 · VISUAL LESSON

Python approximates the integral with small midpoint rectangles

Python · midpoint integration of a normal PDF 10 lines · standard library · CPU-tested
from math import exp, pi, sqrt
def normal_pdf(x):
    return exp(-x*x/2)/sqrt(2*pi)
def integrate(a, b, n=20000):
    dx = (b-a)/n
    return sum(normal_pdf(a+(i+0.5)*dx)*dx for i in range(n))
print('f(0):', round(normal_pdf(0), 6))
print('P(-1<Z<1):', round(integrate(-1, 1), 6))
print('total [-8,8]:', round(integrate(-8, 8), 6))
print('P(Z=0):', 0.0)
Verified output: f(0): 0.398942; P(-1<Z<1): 0.682689; total [-8,8]: 1.0; P(Z=0): 0.0. The “total” is the approximation on [-8,8], rounded to six decimals; the mathematical total over the real line is exactly 1. No external dependencies.

Numerical integration approximates area by adding narrow rectangles. The midpoint rule evaluates the PDF at each subinterval center and multiplies by its width. More slices can reduce integration error for a smooth density. A probability at a single exact point stays zero.

questions.stem: How does a continuous PDF change under the transformation Y=2X+1 when X is uniform on [0,1], and why is an inverse-derivative scaling factor needed?
options: The support of Y changes to [1,3], but its PDF keeps height one because a linear transformation preserves the probability attached to every input value. The total area therefore doubles and is renormalized after observation.
The support becomes [1,3] and the density becomes 0.5 because fY(y)=fX((y−1)/2)×|d((y−1)/2)/dy|. Stretching the interval doubles width, so density must halve to keep probability one.

The support becomes [1,3] and the density becomes two because the forward derivative dY/dX=2 multiplies the original density. The transformed distribution therefore puts twice as much probability in equal-width intervals.
The support becomes [2,4] because multiplying X by two shifts its lower endpoint to two before adding one. Its PDF is 0.5 on that range, preserving area but applying the offset incorrectly.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A one-to-one differentiable transformation changes both the support and the density. With Y=2X+1, the inverse is X=(Y−1)/2 and the absolute inverse derivative is 1/2. Thus X uniform on [0,1] becomes Y uniform on [1,3] with density 0.5, preserving total area one. For example, a machine maps a normalized sensor value to a score on a two-unit scale; an interval of length one inside [1,3] has probability 0.5. Multiplying by the forward derivative would incorrectly double probability.
questions.figure:
06 · VISUAL LESSON

Stretching a random variable spreads the same probability over more units

Input distributionUniform [0,1], density 1, and total area 1.
Output distributionUniform [1,3], density 0.5, and total area 1.

When Y=2X+1, the inverse transformation is X=(Y−1)/2. The change-of-variables rule multiplies the old density by the absolute derivative of the inverse, which is one half. The support changes from [0,1] to [1,3], doubling width while preserving total probability.

questions.tag: Advanced · Joint, marginal and conditional PDFs
questions.stem: For joint density f(x,y)=2 on 0<y<x<1 and zero elsewhere, how do you derive the marginal and conditional densities, and what is P(Y<X/2)?
options: Integrating over y gives fX(x)=2x; dividing the joint density by this marginal gives fY|X(y|x)=1/x for 0<y<x. The triangular region Y<X/2 has total probability 0.5.
Integrating the joint density over the whole unit square gives fX(x)=2 for every x, while conditioning leaves fY|X(y|x)=2. The triangular event Y<X/2 therefore has probability one.
The marginal fX(x)=2x is correct, but the conditional density is 2x because conditioning multiplies rather than divides by the marginal. The region Y<X/2 then has probability 0.25.
The marginal fX(x)=2(1−x) because y ranges from x to one, and the conditional density must be uniform on [x,1]. The event Y<X/2 falls outside that support, giving probability zero.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A joint PDF gives probability per unit area for two continuous variables. Integrating f(x,y)=2 over y from zero to x gives marginal fX(x)=2x. A joint density lives over an area; marginal and conditional densities use slices

A joint PDF gives density over pairs of continuous values; probability is a double integral over a region. Marginalizing integrates out one variable. Conditioning divides the joint density by the marginal where it is positive. The triangular support also shows X and Y are dependent.
